explanations.explanation: Paul says the ignorance is “…due to the hardness of their hearts.” The cause he names is the heart. Picture a cookie that sat in the oven way too long. You could hit it with a rolling pin and it would just laugh at you.
I get why this one tempts you, friend. It sounds like something you'd blame on a family recipe. But Paul never mentions customs here. He says the ignorance is “…due to the hardness of their hearts.”

Idols feel like the obvious suspect, don't they? But Paul doesn't name them in these verses. He says the ignorance in them is “…due to the hardness of their hearts.” Sometimes the answer is sitting right there in the sentence, and I still walk past it like a man looking for his hat while wearing it.

Paul says they've given themselves over “…with a craving for more.” That craving never says "okay, that's enough." It just asks again. I've been caught at the cooling rack with crumbs on my mustache, so believe me, I know what a craving looks like.
Paul says the opposite. What he names is “…a craving for more.” A craving like that isn't quiet at all. It keeps knocking.
I wish that were the line, friend, but Paul doesn't say they wished to stop. He says they had “…a craving for more.” That's a craving pushing forward, not one winding down.

Paul says it plainly: “But this is not the way you came to know Christ.” He's setting the believers' road next to the Gentiles' road, and they don't match. He is not saying it with a smirk, either. He's reminding them who taught them.

Paul says the opposite. His words are, “But this is not the way you came to know Christ.” After describing how the Gentiles live, he turns and tells the believers that way isn't how they learned Christ. So the statement is true, and the answer is the other button.

explanations.answer: The truth that is in Jesus
explanations.explanation: Paul says they were taught “…in keeping with the truth that is in Jesus.” The teaching lined up with Him. Think of a stamp that matches its cutter edge for edge. That's what it looks like when teaching and truth fit.

Paul doesn't mention Greek wisdom here. He says they were taught “…in keeping with the truth that is in Jesus.” The measuring stick is Jesus, not a famous thinker. I'd have picked a fancy answer too, because fancy ones always look good in a hat.
That one sounds respectable, I'll give it that. But Paul doesn't say it. The believers were taught “…in keeping with the truth that is in Jesus.”

Paul says to put off “your former way of life, your old self.” Two names for one thing, and both get taken off. That's step one in his three steps. Honestly, I'd be happy to take off my old self, because my younger days came with a 25 cent price sticker.
Close in warmth, but that isn't what Paul says. He calls the former way of life “your old self.” Nothing about love in that line, friend. It's the self that gets put off.

I see why "younger days" sounds right, since "former" is in the verse. But Paul isn't talking about age. He calls it “your old self.” Trust me, I've got plenty of younger days I'd like to forget, and none of them were what Paul meant.
It's the other way around. Paul says the old self is “being corrupted by its deceitful desires.” Honest and deceitful are opposites. So the desires are called deceitful, not honest.

Right, friend. Paul calls those desires “deceitful.” The full line says the old self “is being corrupted by its deceitful desires.” Honest desires would be easy to follow. Deceitful ones sound good while they're leading you off the counter.

Paul says they were taught “to be renewed in the spirit of your minds.” That's step two, and it happens in the mind. Taking off the old self is one move. Being renewed is another. Right here a lot of folks, me included, want to skip straight to the new apron.
Homes would be easier to renovate, friend, because you can see the walls. But Paul says “minds.” The renewing is in the spirit of the mind, not the house.
Paul doesn't say a word about fathers in this line. The renewal is “in the spirit of your minds.” It's something that happens inside the believers themselves.

Paul says the new self is “created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness.” The pattern is God Himself. That's a big step up from the old self. I can only say, wow, and then say it again, wow.

Abraham, whom God called out of his homeland (Genesis 12:1), is a giant of the faith. But Paul doesn't name him here. He says the new self is created to be like God. That's the pattern, and it's much taller than any one person.

Moses, whom God sent to bring Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10), had an amazing story. Still, Paul doesn't set him as the pattern in this verse. The new self is “created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness.” Not a man, but God Himself.

explanations.answer: We are all members of one another
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Paul gives: “for we are all members of one another.” We're connected, so a lie to your neighbor is really a lie inside the family. It's like a team where one player lies about the score. Everybody ends up playing the wrong game.

explanations.answer: We will all stand before the Lord
explanations.explanation: That's a true idea elsewhere, but it isn't Paul's reason in this verse. He says to speak truthfully “for we are all members of one another.” The reason is how closely we're joined together.

explanations.answer: Our words are weighed by God
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't give that reason here. His reason is “for we are all members of one another.” The stress is on how we belong to each other, friend.
Not quite. The line is “Be angry, yet do not sin.” It doesn't say never be angry. It says that when anger comes, don't let it lead into sin.
Right. The line is “Be angry, yet do not sin.” It doesn't forbid anger. It draws a line around what you do with it. I would've guessed "never," because I've burned a batch and I know how that goes.

explanations.answer: Don't let the sun set on it
explanations.explanation: Paul says, “Do not let the sun set upon your anger.” That's the deadline, and it's short. Anger doesn't get to move in for the night. It has to be dealt with before the day is done.
Three days is generous, friend, but Paul doesn't say it. His line is “Do not let the sun set upon your anger.” The deadline is sundown, not the end of the week.
That sounds like a deadline with some religion in it, but Paul doesn't mention the Sabbath. He says, “Do not let the sun set upon your anger.” The clock here is the sun.
Paul says, “and do not give the devil a foothold.” A foothold is a small place to stand. It's like a toe in the door. Paul's warning is to keep that door from being given even that much room.
Neighbor makes sense, since Paul has just been talking about neighbors. But this line says, “and do not give the devil a foothold.” The foothold isn't for a neighbor. It's one you don't hand over.
I get the guess, since the passage is full of people living together. But the line reads, “and do not give the devil a foothold.” Not a brother, friend, the devil.

explanations.answer: To have something to share with the one in need
explanations.explanation: Paul says he must work, “that he may have something to share with the one in need.” The work isn't just for himself. It ends up as something he can give. The text gives him a good reason to roll up his sleeves.

explanations.answer: To pay back everyone he ever stole from
explanations.explanation: That would be a fair thing to do, but Paul doesn't say it here. The reason he gives is “that he may have something to share with the one in need.” The aim is sharing.

explanations.answer: To earn back his good name around town
explanations.explanation: I can see why that one tempts, friend. Everyone wants a good name. But Paul doesn't give that reason. He says to work “that he may have something to share with the one in need.”

explanations.answer: Only what is helpful for building up
explanations.explanation: Paul says, “but only what is helpful for building up the one in need and bringing grace to those who listen.” Words are meant to build, like a good hand on a wobbling shelf. That's a high bar for the mouth. I'm still working on it myself.
Comfortable sounds nice, friend, but that isn't what Paul says. He says the talk should be “only what is helpful for building up.” Building up and keeping comfortable aren't always the same job.

explanations.answer: Only what shows how much you know
explanations.explanation: Honestly, I'd be tempted by that one, since I love to show off a good stamp. But Paul's standard is “only what is helpful for building up the one in need.” It's about helping the listener, not impressing them.
Yes. Paul says helpful talk is for “bringing grace to those who listen.” So good words don't just sit there. They give something to the person hearing them.
Actually, Paul does say it. The talk is for “building up the one in need and bringing grace to those who listen.” So the statement is true. Helpful words carry grace to the listeners.

That's exactly what Paul says. The Holy Spirit is the one “in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.” So the warning not to grieve Him comes with this reminder of what the believers have in Him.

This one does come right out of the verse. Paul says the believers were sealed in the Holy Spirit of God “for the day of redemption.” So the statement is true. It's why he says, “And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God.”

explanations.answer: Just as in Christ God forgave them
explanations.explanation: Paul says to forgive each other “just as in Christ God forgave you.” That's the pattern for it. We forgive the way we were forgiven. And honestly, friend, that makes the grudge drawer feel a lot smaller.

explanations.answer: As each one confesses his sin
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't set that condition. He says forgive each other “just as in Christ God forgave you.” The measuring stick is how God forgave us in Christ.

explanations.answer: Seven times and then no more
explanations.explanation: That number comes from Peter, one of Jesus' disciples, who asked Jesus if seven times was enough. Jesus told him seventy-seven times (Matthew 18:21-22). In Paul's verse there's no counting at all. He says to forgive “just as in Christ God forgave you.”
